segments_and_separable_assets: Aerospace: Pratt & Whitney engine aftermarket and aerospace systems [D01, D06]
economics_vs_peers: Aerospace segment benefits from recurring aftermarket demand but faces new-platform cash consumption [D01, D06].
Elevator service should be benchmarked against Kone and Schindler; climate products against HVAC peers; aerospace against propulsion/systems suppliers [D06].
management_board_governance: Gregory Hayes chairs and leads the company [D01].

Potential for portfolio structure review/separation (not currently approved) [D01, D06, D07].

Low near-term free cash flow conversion [D05].

gate1.edge_statement: Third Point identifies the conglomerate discount and the potential for a value-unlocking separation of distinct industrial units, utilizing peer-based benchmarking to drive portfolio simplification.
gate1.one_line_verdict: a diversified industrial conglomerate with high-quality separable units that can be unlocked through a structured separation strategy.

gate2.variant_view: The market views the company as a complex, diversified conglomerate suffering from poor free cash flow conversion and execution risk in its aerospace division, resulting in a persistent valuation discount. We believe the sum-of-the-parts value is significantly higher, as the company owns three world-class businesses that should be separated to unlock their true earnings potential and valuation multiples. A strategic separation will allow investors to realize the full value of the aerospace, elevator, and climate assets independently [D01, D06].

The aerospace segment, while high-quality, is obscured by the broader conglomerate structure [D01, D06].

The separation can be executed in a tax-efficient manner.
Operational performance in the aerospace business remains stable enough to support a standalone valuation.
Management is willing to engage in a structured portfolio simplification process.

final.memo:
The Company is a diversified industrial conglomerate whose true potential is masked by its current structure, leading to a persistent and unnecessary conglomerate discount [D01, D06]. While the aerospace, elevator, and climate businesses are world-class, they are currently managed as a single entity, which we believe is an inefficient way to extract value for shareholders [D01, D06].

Our sum-of-the-parts analysis reveals a compelling upside. By benchmarking the elevator business against peers like Kone and Schindler, and valuing the aerospace and climate units against their respective sectors at an average 14.0x EBITDA multiple, we derive a valuation of $160 per share [D03, D06]. This stands in stark contrast to the current $120.15 trading price, which fails to recognize the independent earnings power of the core segments [D04].

The market’s focus on temporary execution risks in the aerospace segment and historical conglomerate complexity has created this mispricing [D01, D05]. We believe that a strategic, tax-efficient separation into three independent, public companies is the necessary catalyst to unlock this value [D01, D06]. Transparency as standalone entities will force the market to assign market-appropriate multiples to each business rather than the current depressed conglomerate stub [D01].

We are engaging privately with Chairman and CEO Gregory Hayes to outline our proposal for this separation [D01, D07]. We expect management to commit to segment-specific margin targets and provide a roadmap for structural independence within two quarters [D06, D07]. Should management remain unresponsive to this constructive approach, we are prepared to take our case directly to shareholders [D07].

We see a hard valuation floor at $115 per share, based on current EBITDA and a 11.0x multiple, which supports a highly asymmetric 33%:4% risk/reward skew [D03, D04]. Our downside risk is limited by the recurring aftermarket revenue in the aerospace division [D01, D05]. We intend to build a 7% position in the common stock to capitalize on this event-driven opportunity [D04].
